item.title: MITRE ATTCK Heatmap for Splunk - v1.11.0 [Version Update]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
### v1.11.0 **New** - A new look: flat tactic headers with a coverage figure and gauge, connected cells, hatching for techniques with no value, and a tooltip and legend that follow Splunk's light and dark themes - Color bands (3, 5, 7 or 9) with a legend that has a *No data* entry, a *Palette* option (Default, Risk, Sequential blues, Viridis) and perceptual color blending - A new tooltip with the band and rank, the other tactics a technique is in, and clickable sub-techniques; click a cell to pin it - Search that also matches sub-technique names, descriptions and tactic names; keyboard navigation; messages for empty results, unmatched IDs and rows without values - Search text, the pinned band, tactic or tooltip, and the scroll position are kept when the search refreshes - Map result columns by name (*ID field*, *Value field*, *Description field*, *Status field*) - *Roll up sub-techniques*, *Color bounds: From data*, status-based coloring, and an ATT&CK Navigator export button - *Matrix data: Imported*, with a scripted input and a report that download newer ATT&CK versions - *Wall mode* for display walls - Bundled data updated to ATT&CK v20.0 - Dashboard Studio: defaults match classic dashboards, and the export shows a copy box **Changed** - D3FEND follows the current ontology: seven tactic columns (Model, Harden, Detect, Isolate, Deceive, Evict, Restore), 30 techniques and 241 sub-techniques with their own IDs. Dashboards that match on D3FEND tactic names or IDs in drilldown tokens need updating (for example `d3f:Harden`) - ATT&CK v20 replaced the Enterprise tactic *Defense Evasion* with *Stealth* and *Defense Impairment*; drilldowns that match on that name need updating - The default panel height is 1200 pixels (it was 2700) - Panels that are too small now scroll instead of squeezing the columns - *Sort by* now defaults to Value, Descending - The entrance animation is always on, once when the panel first loads - The legend title is always the value field's name; the menu is smaller and grouped into Data, Display, Colors, Scale and Export **Removed** - The *Theme* option (the heatmap follows the dashboard's theme), the *Animate* and *Duration* options, *Legend title*, and the sweeping highlight animation **Fixed** - Enterprise tactic order for v20, several heatmaps on one dashboard affecting each other, *Hide empty* removing sub-techniques that have values, zero and decimal values in tooltips, searching for names that contain `&`, one click sending several drilldowns, and several platform choices that showed an empty matrix - Text built from field names in the legend is now escaped


Short Description:
Custom visualization that renders MITRE ATT&CK and D3FEND matrices as interactive heatmaps, coloring techniques by search result values to reveal detection coverage, gaps, and hot spots.


Description:
The MITRE ATT&CK Heatmap for Splunk is a custom visualization that transforms search results into interactive MITRE ATT&CK or D3FEND matrices. The visualization colors each technique based on numeric values returned by a search query, enabling security teams to visualize detection coverage, identify gaps, and highlight areas of concentrated activity. The app supports the ATT&CK Enterprise, ICS, and Mobile frameworks, as well as the D3FEND framework. It ships with bundled matrix data (ATT&CK v20.0 and D3FEND v1.6.0) and includes an optional scripted input that automatically imports newer ATT&CK versions from the MITRE GitHub repository. The visualization integrates with both Simple XML and Dashboard Studio, providing drilldown capabilities and export options. Users format the heatmap by selecting the framework, domain, color scale bounds, and whether to use bundled or imported matrix data.

item.title: Supply Chain and AI Threat Intelligence Platform - v1.2.18 [New App Release]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
## SCIP v1.2.18 — Role-Aware Gateway Content, Prompt-Injection Pattern Accuracy, and OSV Range Matching This release supersedes v1.2.17 and carries forty fixes and improvements across AI and LLM threat detection, vulnerability matching accuracy, and deployment documentation. No configuration changes or manual steps are required on upgrade. No detection severity value or MITRE ATLAS technique mapping changed. **AI and LLM gateway coverage:** - Kong AI Gateway request payloads are now parsed and routed by message role across all three of Kong's logging key layouts, so prompt content is separated into user, system, assistant and tool channels instead of being evaluated as one blended string. - Kong AI Gateway responses now reach the role-aware assistant channel. Three response-reading detections, including LLM Sensitive Information Disclosure, previously returned nothing at all on Kong traffic. - user_input is assembled per message role on every supported gateway, so a detection targeting user-supplied prompt content no longer matches on system or assistant text. - LiteLLM deployments behind a load balancer now attribute activity to the real caller when the documented IP-forwarding step is configured. That documented step previously had no effect and attribution fell back to the balancer. - Gateway attribution fields are normalised consistently across the supported gateways, and the gateways where a field is not yet established are recorded as such rather than assumed. **Detection accuracy:** - Six detection stanzas no longer match on bare over-broad words such as "override" and "disregard", which fired on ordinary operational text. They now match the injection shape plus a tiered set of retained literals. - Prompt-injection patterns now match every "verb + qualifier + previous instructions" phrasing rather than a fixed list of phrases. - Two detections were rewritten away from literal phrase matching to shape-based patterns. - The credential-harvesting detection no longer fires on ordinary security advice. - Repeated injection attempts by one actor within one session no longer raise duplicate alerts. - LLM Cache Poisoning can now fire, because its gate read fields the rule never received. - Two detections carried pattern alternatives that could never match. Both are corrected, with regression fixtures added. - 68 ATLAS detections now surface the confidence value they already computed, bringing all 75 that compute one to carry it through to the alert. **Vulnerability matching:** - Advisories that express several affected version ranges for one package are now matched against every range. Previously only the first range was kept, so a component inside any later range was reported as not vulnerable. - Exact affected-version lists are now read for advisories that carry no machine-readable range. - Git commit hashes are no longer presented as upgrade targets, and the fix-availability state now distinguishes "no fix published" from "fix recorded only as a commit". - The bundled vulnerability seed and the live OSV feed both now cover all eleven documented ecosystems. The seed previously drew from five and the live feed polled eight. - Repository-qualified ecosystem values no longer reach the lookup. All three writers normalise the value, and an affected install corrects itself on its next scheduled run. - Severity grading in the bundled seed is restored. The offline generator carried an older severity parser that graded roughly 90 percent of rows as unknown. - The bundled snapshot date shown on the Home dashboard is written alongside the seed, so it can no longer report a date the seed does not match. - On licensed tiers the live OSV feed hands off to the vulnerability lookup automatically once it holds data, with no manual step. The Home dashboard freshness indicator derives its state from the lookup contents and adds a "lookup behind live feed" state. **Platform and documentation:** - The vendored Splunk SDK for Python is upgraded to 3.0.1. - Supported Splunk version statements are aligned across the app and its documentation. - The air-gapped and IL deployment guides are corrected. The OSV feed is now listed in the egress-disable procedure, the customer seed refresh procedure specifies the extraction rules it previously omitted, and the stated Python requirement for the offline seed generator is corrected. **Upgrade notes:** - No manual steps, configuration changes or saved-search edits are required. - Component vulnerability counts may rise after upgrade. Advisories with several affected version ranges were previously matched against the first range only, so components inside a later range were reported as not vulnerable. Those components now match correctly. Risk scores, dashboard counts and remediation rows reflect the corrected matching. - Installs running the live OSV feed on a licensed tier correct the ecosystem value in the lookup on the next scheduled run. No licensing or crypto surface was modified in this release. bin/scip_license_core.py and bin/scip_ed25519_verify.py are byte-identical to baseline.


Short Description:
A Splunk app that detects AI-threat patterns (MITRE ATLAS) and runs software composition analysis (SCA) on your SBOMs to identify known-vulnerable components (NVD, OSV) — surfacing the applications where both appear at once. Compliance evidence across nine frameworks and FedRAMP/RMF audit exports, with no separate platform to stand up.


Description:
SCIP is a Splunk app that detects adversarial AI/ML threats (MITRE ATLAS) and runs software composition analysis (SCA) on your SBOMs to identify known-vulnerable components (NVD, OSV) — then, through Compound Risk, surfaces the applications where an AI-threat detection and a known vulnerability appear at once, the exposure neither signal shows alone. It prioritizes with CISA KEV and EPSS and assesses compliance posture across nine frameworks — detection logic written as transparent SPL you can open and read, and no separate platform to stand up. AI THREAT DETECTION - MITRE ATLAS Detection — 81 AI/agentic threat detection rules (72 mapped to 57 MITRE ATLAS techniques) - Compound Risk — correlates MITRE ATLAS AI-threat detections with KEV-listed or critical-severity vulnerabilities on the same application - Silent-Source Detection — alerts when an enrolled AI/LLM telemetry source goes quiet, so a dead pipe is never mistaken for a clean one - AI/ML Bill of Materials — catalogs AI/ML model components from your SBOMs with insecure-serialization-format flagging and risk classification SOFTWARE SUPPLY CHAIN - SBOM ingestion — file-drop or HEC, supporting CycloneDX (JSON/XML) and SPDX (JSON) - Vulnerability correlation — bundled OSV dataset (250,000+ records across 11 ecosystems) with PURL-based correlation, refreshed daily from the live OSV feed across 8 configurable ecosystems; NVD CPE-based correlation; CISA KEV matching; EPSS scoring - Supply Chain Risk Score — 0–100 global and per-application scoring weighted by severity, KEV status, and EPSS - Vendor Risk — per-vendor risk aggregation and letter-grading - SBOM Drift Detection — baseline-vs-current component change tracking - Long-Unpatched Critical Exposure — flags critical/high-severity vulnerabilities unpatched 180+ days - License Compliance — GPL/AGPL/copyleft detection and license-risk classification COMPLIANCE, FEDERAL & AIR-GAPPED DEPLOYMENT - Air-gapped operation — AI-threat detection runs on your own Splunk data, SBOM correlation on the bundled OSV dataset, and intelligence feeds refresh by file transfer rather than live calls; deployed disconnected, SCIP makes no outbound connections - Compliance Gap Assessment — nine frameworks: PCI DSS 4.0.1, NIST CSF 2.0, SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA Security Rule, EU Cyber Resilience Act, FedRAMP / RMF / CISA, DORA, FDA 524B Premarket Cybersecurity, SEBI CSCRF - POA&M & FedRAMP Workflow — POA&M dashboard, monthly ConMon package builder, BOD 26-04 risk-tier classification, deviation request workflow. Dashboards always available; automated POA&M generation is opt-in from Setup - Coverage-Evidence Manifest — AU-12-aligned attestation of unbroken AI-monitoring coverage - Audit-ready exports — FedRAMP POA&M Workbook, SSP Appendix M Integrated Inventory, Deviation Request Form

item.title: HoneyLabs Intelligence - v1.2.2 [New App Release]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
The app icons and logo use the current HoneyLabs mark. The fingerprint types are ja4, ja3, akin and hassh. The app, its threat feeds and address enrichment are free to use; a free API key raises the daily lookup cap and opens the dataset search command.


Short Description:
Free threat intelligence from live honeypot sensors, in SPL. Enrich any IP field with a verdict, ASN, ports and first and last seen, or query the dataset directly: raw probes, request payloads, CVE exploitation, JA4 fingerprints, top attackers. Plus two hourly threat feeds. No account needed; a free API key raises lookups from 10 to 500 a day.


Description:
Free to use. The app and both threat feeds work without an account, and a free API key raises the daily lookup cap. HoneyLabs runs open-source honeypot sensors on the public internet. Nothing reaches them by accident, so every connection they record is a scan, a probe, a brute-force attempt or an exploit. There are no false positives to filter out, because there is no legitimate traffic to confuse them with. This app puts that dataset inside Splunk. Two search commands. The first enriches addresses you already have. Point it at any field holding a public IPv4 address and it annotates every event: index=firewall | honeylabs field=src_ip | where honeylabs_events > 0 It writes back verdict, verdict_key, network_type, events, first_seen, last_seen, country, asn, asn_org, rdns, top_port, ports, exploit_hits and reference, each prefixed honeylabs_ so nothing collides with your own fields. Addresses are de-duplicated per search, so an index carrying the same scanner across ten thousand events costs one lookup. The second queries the honeypot dataset directly, with no local data required. Nine modes cover raw events, captured request payloads, top attackers, timelines, ASN profiles, TLS and HTTP fingerprints, IOC and CIDR lookups, CVE exploitation, and fingerprint population counts. Use it to answer questions your own logs cannot: who else is exercising this CVE, what payload is being sent, which other sources share this JA4 fingerprint. Two modular inputs, shipped disabled, index active exploiter addresses and captured malware staging URLs on an hourly schedule. Neither needs credentials. Two dashboards ship with the app: an overview of what the feeds currently carry, and an explorer for querying the dataset without writing SPL by hand. About the API key. The app installs and runs with no account and no setup, but anonymous use is capped at 10 lookups a day, which is enough to try the commands and not enough to work with. A free key raises that to 500 a day and takes about a minute to create at https://honeylabs.net/dashboard. Paste it into the app's setup page; it is stored through Splunk's storage/passwords, encrypted at rest, and never written to a .conf file. Paid plans go to 50,000 a day. On privacy: a lookup sends only the public IP addresses in your search. Not your index, host, source or sourcetype names, not your Splunk version, not the search string. Private, loopback, link-local, multicast and reserved addresses are filtered out locally before the request is built. The feed inputs are ordinary HTTPS downloads of a public file and disclose nothing at all. Running Enterprise Security? Load the indicator feeds through its own threat intelligence framework so they reach correlation searches and risk scoring rather than only being searchable, and keep these commands for on-demand investigation. Walkthrough: https://honeylabs.net/integrations/splunk-es

item.title: Adjutant AI - v2.7.5 [New App Release]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
# Adjutant AI (formerly AI Workbench) — Release notes What's new, improved, and fixed in each release, in plain language. This is the **customer-facing** summary used for the Splunkbase release-notes section; the full technical changelog lives in the project's detailed release notes. **Last updated:** 2026-10-28 > **About version numbers.** Releases once numbered 0.10–0.13 were renumbered to > 1.0–1.3 to reflect production maturity — no behaviour changed. The current release is > **2.7.5**, a maintenance release on **2.7.0** after **2.7.1**, **2.7.2** and **2.7.3**: Adjutant AI runs **governed agents**, a **Tool calls** panel shows each step of a > request and lets you stop it, and **multi-source reconciliation** arrives as a Preview. > 2.7.0 sits on top of **2.5.9**'s setup wizard that says which model actually answered and why a > gateway lists none, a ninth option for self-hosted and in-house models, and connection checks that > no longer award a pass they did not earn; 2.5.9 on top of **2.5.8**'s playbooks that carry all of their instructions, and every path to > an AI service agreeing about where a request goes, and 2.5.8 on top of **2.5.4**'s readable RCA report and **2.5.3**'s private LLM endpoints and **2.5.2**'s one connection for several tenants and **2.5.1**'s fixes to **2.5.0**'s setup wizard and **2.4.2** — a data-correctness fix on top of **2.4.1**, a connectivity release on top of the **2.4.0** integration workstream and **2.2.2**, itself a maintenance release on **2.2.1**, itself a maintenance release on > **2.2.0**'s **Explain a SPL search**, and **2.1.0**'s **Fraud capability** and the **2.0 line** (the deterministic **ITSI Root > Cause Analysis** engine, **resource-consumption monitoring**, and **2.0.7**'s durable memory, > Scheduled Ask and governed integrations), which in turn built on > **1.8.5** (the **CIM Coverage Audit**), **1.8.4** (async playbook execution over MCP > plus the **Outcome Ledger** executive/audit dashboard), **1.8.3** > (a security‑hardening release: OWASP + dependency + anti‑ransomware audit), **1.8.2** (Splunk > Edge Processor data‑quality awareness and keyless Azure OpenAI authentication), **1.8.1** > (support‑diagnosis fixes) and **1.8.0** (agent telemetry & OCSF export, content packs, > all‑tiers data‑quality checks, Splunk 10.x readiness, Dashboard Studio version‑awareness). The > **1.7.0** ServiceNow integration and the **1.5.0 "Data Foundation & MCP OAuth"** themes are > included below. --- ## 2.7.5 **In short.** A maintenance release: Settings and the setup wizard now show who may use a connection as it is stored, and saving a connection never changes who may use it unless you choose to. Searches are checked faster and more accurately, Adjutant AI decides how to run a search instead of asking you, and the Tool calls panel shows only what needs your attention. Dashboards publish faster, the check of their panels looks further back for each panel, and a dashboard built with the dashboard builder carries a Data quality row. A cost Adjutant AI cannot know is shown as unknown instead of $0.0000, model prices can be refreshed, and AI Activity is a new analysis view of agent runs. - **The connection list matches what Adjutant AI allows.** The list of AI connections could offer a connection that a request then refused, or leave out one you were allowed to use, for example a connection open to everyone that was created while a different Organisation was selected. The list now offers exactly the connections you may use. - **Settings and the setup wizard show who may use a connection as stored.** "Who may use this connection?" could open on the wrong value, for example "Everyone" for a connection only one Business Unit may use. It now opens on what is stored, and step 4 of the wizard compares your choice with what is stored. - **Editing a connection in Settings keeps who may use it.** Saving a connection from Edit in Settings could move it to the Organisation and Business Unit selected on the Settings page and open it to every Organisation and every Business Unit. It could also remove settings the edit screen does not show. A connection now keeps its own Organisation, Business Unit and access list, and every setting you did not change. If you saved a connection from Edit in Settings before 2.7.5, check who may use it. - **Adjutant AI decides how to run a search, and says what it did.** When a search filters on a field that exists only at search time, Adjutant AI now checks the fast form against the exact one itself, uses the fast one only when both find the same events in a recent sample, and says which it used and why. It no longer asks you to choose a technique. - **Checking a search for rare events is quicker.** It first finds when they happened, then checks only the few minutes around it, so the check stays quick on large clusters. - **A quick look at raw events over a long period stops after the events it shows**, instead of reading the whole period. - **The Tool calls panel shows only what needs your attention.** A search you cancelled, and time spent waiting for your approval, are no longer marked as slow. A problem Adjutant AI caught and corrected in the same answer is shown as corrected, not as something to look at. - **The answer check says when a rewrite did not fix what it found**, instead of reporting a rewrite. A link it could not confirm is still shown under the answer. - **Publishing a dashboard is quicker.** The checks that run before a dashboard is published now run a few at a time instead of one after another, and a finished check is noticed sooner. - **Replacing an existing dashboard always asks you first.** Earlier versions could replace an existing dashboard without asking: when Adjutant AI published or compiled a dashboard with overwrite on, or revised a dashboard, the dashboard was replaced with no confirmation. Each of these now asks first in "Allow a write action", which shows the tool and its arguments, and nothing is written unless you allow it. If Adjutant AI cannot ask you, it does not replace the dashboard. Publishing a dashboard under a new name does not ask. - **Fewer warnings in splunkd.log.** Adjutant AI waits a moment before it first reads a new search's status, and when it runs several searches at once it starts them one after another; they still run side by side. Splunk logged "could not read metadata file" when several searches were started at the same instant. - **Checking a dashboard's panels looks further back for each panel on its own.** A panel with no data in the last hour is checked over the last 24 hours and then its full time range, even when other panels did have data in that hour, and the result says which period found its data. Small indexes named with a wildcard, such as `demo*`, are now checked without sampling. - **A published dashboard carries a Data quality row.** When Adjutant AI builds a Simple XML dashboard with its dashboard builder, publishing pins a Data quality row at the top: the ingestion check for the sourcetypes its panels read (counts only) and the newest event per index. If no event arrived in the last 24 hours, the row says so. If the check cannot run, it says "not checked" and why. It is an administrator feature of the **Enterprise** edition and above, driven through the app's REST interface (`/services/itmip_recon`). A run goes through five steps: 1. **Stage** each source's rows into a holding area. 2. **Accept** a source's data as a whole, or reject it as a whole: enough rows, a usable key on every row, no duplicate keys. A read the source reports as **truncated**, or one that lost more rows than the contract allows, is still accepted for what it saw — but it is never used to decide that something is gone. 3. **Reconcile** the accepted data. Every run leaves a record with a verdict — complete, incomplete or refused — and the reason. 4. **Request and approve.** A complete run becomes the approved view only when **a second administrator** approves it. Approving your own request is refused, and who approved is taken from the Splunk session, never from what the request says. 5. **Promote.** The approved run becomes the current view, and the baseline the next run compares against. **It refuses rather than guesses**, and says why: - When a contract names a holding area for its sources, a reconciliation reads only data that was accepted in step 2, and rows sent with the request are refused. - An organisation's first run is reported as a first run. A lookup table never adds a record of its own, each enriched value names the table it came from, and the run reports how much of the table matched nothing. **Renames.** When a record's key changes and nothing else identifies it, reconciliation treats it as a new record. An administrator can record that the two are the same thing (a *rekey*); a second administrator must approve it, and the old record then keeps its history under the new one instead of being reported as gone. **Freshness and trust per source.** Every run records, for each source, whether it was read recently enough and whether it may report that something is gone — each with a named reason when the answer is no. ### Changed: who may approve a blocked integration write - **Only the person who requested a blocked write, or an administrator, may now see, approve or cancel it.** **Power users can no longer approve other users' runs**; ask the requester or an administrator. Every retirement and deletion is read back. **ServiceNow as a source.** A contract can also *read* a ServiceNow table as one of its sources (`stage_servicenow`): the table is read in full through the organisation's ServiceNow connection, filtered as the contract declares, and staged like any other source; when it is accepted, it takes part in reconciliation. A view takes its table's role from that declaration; a view on a read-only table, a removal on a written table, or two views claiming the same authoritative table is refused before anything is sent, and reported on the reconciliation run. **Held runs.** For a table the integration is authoritative for, a live run is **held** — nothing is written — when the view would publish nothing, when it is the view's first live run, when its output is below the usual size of its recent verified runs, or when it would remove more than 10% of the records the integration owns there (adjustable per view). An administrator approves or rejects the held run (`approve_held` / `reject_held`, naming its preview); who decided, and when, is recorded, and every check is written to the safeguard log. **Checked after every live run.** For an authoritative table, Adjutant reads the table back: the records the integration owns must be exactly the records the view published, field by field. A difference is reported by record and field, and the run is recorded as not verified. Records in the table that the integration does not own are never touched; they are counted and reported. **A recent write test is required.** Before the first live run, and again every 7 days, an administrator runs the write-capability test (`capability_test`): Adjutant writes one test record to a table you name, checks that ServiceNow kept its source attribution, and removes it again. Records written that way by an earlier version stay where they are; remove them yourself if you do not want them. - **Only what changed is read.** After its first run, an integration reads only the records that changed since the last run it verifiably wrote, and its run says so ("no row changed since …"). - **Record values stay out of the AI model.** Adjutant makes the read itself and hands the model a reference to the records, never the records. They are planned for a 2.7.x update. ## 2.5.9 The setup wizard now tells you which model actually answered your question, and says plainly when a gateway publishes no model list, instead of showing a bare error. "Does not apply" was the correct verdict. What made it read as a fault of ours is that the row showed the bare 404 next to it and no reason, so a property of their gateway looked like a gap in the product. The row now says the endpoint publishes no model list. **But the run had already learned the model and was throwing it away.** The check below it asks a real question, and the reply names the model that answered it. Most of what follows was found by opening a diagnostic package and comparing the two. ### Playbooks were running without most of their instructions **This affected every playbook run from the Ask tab, and it is the reason to take this release.** A playbook is a short procedure plus a set of reusable **skills** it declares: the rules on correctness traps, performance priorities, evidence, naming, and so on. Picking a playbook from the Ask screen sent the procedure and none of the skills. It was invisible from either end. A playbook declaring nine skills produced a prompt byte for byte identical to one declaring none, and nothing reported a skill as missing. Each had grown its own answer to questions all four have to agree on, and the checks were the path that happened to be right. The result was an `AttributeError` on every request, surfaced as a generic internal error with the real reason only in `splunkd.log`. The orchestrator is restored alongside the newer retry helper. The two are disjoint and stay that way: one is the writer's bounded per-request retry, the other is the provider fallback chain with its circuit breaker and per-attempt journal. `tests/test_llm_retry.py` covers the restored path and was failing on `import` for two releases, which is how this reached a release at all. ### Network-policy events were merged, not split When a device snapshot was stored to a Splunk index, every rule from that device arrived as a **single event** containing the whole batch of JSON records, instead of one event per rule. The field list still showed `rule_id`, `action`, `source_values` and the rest, because Splunk extracts fields from the first JSON object in an event — so the fields you clicked on were real and correct. Only the **count** was wrong, and the counts the app itself reported were counts of records submitted, not of events landed. A `| stats count by device_id` over the rule source type therefore under-reported by however many rules a device had. The cause was a single character. `default/props.conf` declared the parsing rules under `[adjutant:network_policy:*]`, and props.conf applies its wildcard match language to `source::` and `host::` stanzas only — in a source-type stanza the `*` is literal, so the stanza matched nothing and the events fell back to Splunk's defaults. Each family now has its own stanza, and a `[source::itmip_llm_splunk_writer]` stanza backstops any source type added to that path in future. ### A policy field was colliding with one of Splunk's own Expanded policy tuples carry a field named `source` — and `source` is one of the fields Splunk defines on every event, where it names what wrote the record. Splunk does not overwrite on a collision, it **merges**, so `| table source` returned the policy's source address and `itmip_llm_splunk_writer` together in one cell, with nothing to say which was which. Fields whose names Splunk already owns are now written as `original_` — so that one is `original_source`. This applies to the **index** write only: the KV Store rows, the policy graph and the API keep the model's own names, because `source` is part of what a `tuple_id` is hashed from and renaming it there would move every tuple id ever issued. ### `source` and `host` said who wrote the event, not where the data came from Every network-policy event landed with `source = itmip_llm_splunk_writer` and `host = ai_workbench` — true of every event this app has ever written, and therefore no use for filtering or for a CIM-style view of where a policy came from. To correct history, remove the affected events and re-store the snapshots. --- ## 2.4.1 "Getting connected" Everything here came out of two customer setups in the same fortnight: an Azure OpenAI service published through a corporate API gateway, and one behind a private endpoint. A playbook can take several minutes, but AI tool calls are subject to short timeouts you don't control (the MCP server, the client, proxies), so trying to wait for the answer in one call is fragile. Now every call returns in seconds. **New / Improved** - **Start returns immediately.** `adjutantai_start_playbook` (the old `adjutantai_run_playbook` name is removed) hands back a run id at once with a hint on how to poll. - **Check progress** with `adjutantai_get_playbook_status` — queued, running, completed, or failed (a run that hit a recoverable error and is auto‑retrying is reported as still running, not failed), with guidance to stop polling after ~15 minutes. - **Fetch the verdict** with `adjutantai_get_playbook_results` once completed — condensed by default, or the full result on request; a partial result is clearly labelled. - **Tenant‑safe.** One team can't read another team's run; unknown or expired run ids simply return "not found." Run records are kept for 7 days by default. - **Try it out of the box:** start `MCP Example: Read-only Health Check` under Org/BU `DFLT/DFLT` (the read‑only reference playbook shipped on every install), then poll and fetch. Requires the inbound MCP server and the Backend Ask Service to be enabled. No configuration changes. Restart Splunk after upgrading. ### Also in 1.8.4 — the Outcome Ledger (Enterprise) A single screen that answers what a CEO, CISO or auditor actually asks: *what did agentic AI do for us this period, was it any good, what did it save, what did it cost — and can I see the evidence for one run?* It assembles data the app already records (unattended‑run history, analyst agreement, run telemetry, LLM spend) into one executive/audit view. It adds **no new data collection and sends nothing to any external service.** **New** - **The dashboard** (`Adjutant AI ▸ Outcome Ledger`): headline tiles (investigations run without a human, how often analysts agreed with the AI — with the sample size and coverage shown, benign/false‑positive runs auto‑closed, analyst hours saved, LLM spend, typical time to a verdict), the mix of AI conclusions over time, agreement by case type, a weekly ledger, and an **evidence** table you can click through to the full detail of any single run. A footer spells out every assumption so a number is never quoted out of context. - **Safe to hand to an auditor.** What each viewer may see is decided on the server from their own identity — never from the page — and fails closed. In this release the dashboard is for Splunk administrators; scoped, delegated auditor access is the next step. - **Is the AI real, or just performing?** An Efficacy Trend panel puts run volume against how often analysts agreed, over time. If the agent runs more while analysts increasingly override it, the panel says so ("scaling faster than trust") instead of hiding it behind a healthy‑looking headline — and on too little feedback it honestly says the sample is too thin to judge. - **Honest numbers.** Effort saved is shown as time (with the per‑case assumption stated), spend is the real logged cost, and the per‑investigation efficiency signal is token usage — never an invented cost estimate. Enterprise feature. No effect on any existing behaviour. Restart Splunk after upgrading. --- ## 1.8.3 "Security hardening" A security‑focused release. Adjutant AI was put through an independent OWASP Top 10 (web **and** LLM), dependency‑vulnerability, and "AI‑driven ransomware" review. The headline: **no critical issues, no default passwords or keys, no vulnerable components that ship to you, and the assistant cannot be turned into an attack tool.** Confirmed issues are fixed; a plain‑language, reviewer‑ready write‑up ships in the app as `SECURITY_AUDIT.md`. **Improved / Fixed** - **Credentials stay server‑side.** Provider API keys and keyless Azure sign‑in secrets are never sent to the browser or to other users in your tenant. (The free‑tier browser API‑key path is unchanged.) - **Prompts stay in your audit index**, not Splunk's internal logs. - **Stronger multi‑tenant isolation** for investigation results and knowledge sources. - **You confirm every change.** Closing a notable, setting a disposition, an ITSI/TrackMe/ServiceNow write, or overwriting a saved dashboard now asks for explicit confirmation first. Read‑only questions and new private dashboards are unaffected. - **General hardening:** cleaner errors, tighter sign‑in redirects, safer content‑pack imports, email TLS verification on by default. No new features or config changes. Restart Splunk after upgrading. --- ## 1.8.2 "Edge Processor data-quality + keyless Azure OpenAI auth" **Keyless Azure OpenAI (Microsoft Entra ID / managed identity).** Connect Azure OpenAI **without a static API key** — using a Microsoft Entra ID service principal or a managed identity, governed by your Entra tenant. Runs entirely server-side (no token reaches the browser), supports Public and US Gov clouds, and adds a one-click **Test connection** that names exactly what to fix if something is off. Connecting Azure with a plain **API key** still works on every tier; the keyless Entra path is an **Enterprise** capability. --- ### Edge Processor data-quality If your data passes through **Splunk Edge Processor** before it reaches Splunk, some parsing, timestamping, dropping and routing happens *upstream* — where Splunk's own internal logs and feed-health tools can't see it. This release teaches the assistant to look at that hop. - **New "Edge Processor → Splunk data-quality check".** Ask the assistant to check an Edge Processor feed and it reads Edge Processor's own operational metrics (throughput, dropped events, failed destination sends, and queue backpressure) and tells you, in plain language, whether data is being silently lost or delayed before it lands — with a proof dashboard. - **Honest by design.** If Edge Processor telemetry isn't reaching your Splunk yet, the assistant says so and gives you the exact setup steps (on-premises vs Splunk Cloud) instead of inventing a clean bill of health. It reports at the pipeline level and is clear that per-event checks need a small addition to your Edge Processor pipeline. - **Folds into the readiness verdict.** Edge Processor joins Splunk parsing, feed-health, and Cribl as another "is this data actually good?" signal, and can cap the Data Quality Score when it finds upstream loss. - Read-only and available on every tier, exactly like the existing Cribl check. --- ## 1.8.1 "Cleaner support diagnosis" A small maintenance update over 1.8.0 (front-end only). - **More accurate "Report an issue" diagnosis.** The automated issue classifier no longer mislabels a session that finished normally — one that completed and produced its dashboard — as having "run out of tool steps." The suspected-issue summary in your support bundle is now cleaner for healthy, tool-heavy sessions. --- ## 1.8.0 "Agent telemetry & OCSF export, content packs & all-tiers data quality" **New — your SOC can watch the agent (OCSF telemetry).** - **Adjutant AI emits its own activity as OCSF.** Every LLM call, tool / MCP / ServiceNow call, configuration change, unattended run verdict, and **policy refusal** (the proof the controls actually fire) can be written as open-standard **OCSF** events to a Splunk index your Enterprise Security / SOC already watches — mapped to CIM via the community **OCSF-CIM Add-On**. Your SOC monitors our agent the same way it monitors everything else: on-prem, with no cloud egress. - **You stay in control.** It is **off by default** and Enterprise-gated. **You provision and name the index** (the app ships no `indexes.conf`). Routing and content are resolved **per Organisation / Business Unit**; content export is denied by default and never exceeds your audit (DPIA) ceiling, with a server-side redaction check before anything is written. - **See it immediately.** A shipped admin dashboard — *Adjutant AI — Behaviour (OCSF)* — shows the token trend, model mix, tool/MCP egress with identity, the refusal and finding feeds, and a per-run drilldown, all on raw OCSF (no CIM Add-On required). **New — update Adjutant's content without waiting for a whole new app release.** - **Content packs.** Almost everything Adjutant does well lives in its **content** — the skills, knowledge, and playbooks. A **content pack** is a single, versioned file that lets us ship a corrected or improved content set straight to your install, and lets your admin apply it safely — no Splunkbase re-vetting cycle for a content fix. - **Your changes are protected.** Applying a pack **upgrades only the items you haven't changed**. Anything your team has customised is left exactly as-is and clearly listed, never silently overwritten — and your Org/BU scoping is always preserved. After an import you get a per-item report, and the list of items that need manual reconciliation is downloadable as a CSV. - **Safe by design.** Every pack carries an integrity check, so a tampered or truncated file is refused. Imports live on the **Backups** page, which also shows which content version you're currently on — run a backup first and you can roll back in one click. - **Retire without deleting.** A pack can mark an item **retired** — it stays installed but is hidden and switched off everywhere (it can't be picked, run, or used by the assistant). An admin can re-enable it at any time by removing the tag. **Improved — data-quality checks for everyone, and Splunk 10.x readiness.** - **Data-quality ingestion checks are now available on every edition, including the free tier.** Checking whether a feed is actually landing and parsing correctly — on `index=_internal`, through **TrackMe**, and through **Cribl Stream** — is a baseline capability now, not a Professional add-on. - **Ready for Splunk Enterprise 10.2 and 10.4.** The app declares Python 3.9 **and** 3.13 compatibility and has been audited against the 10.x platform changes (dashboards, the web framework, KV Store). Your admin still completes the standard KV Store engine migration as part of any 10.x upgrade. - **Smarter Dashboard Studio building.** The assistant now works from a single, version-aware map of what Dashboard Studio supports on **your** Splunk version — it won't reach for a chart type your version can't render, and when your Splunk is newer than what we've documented it builds conservatively and verifies the result. **Fixed.** - **Fewer false "the dashboard is blank" errors.** A heavy Dashboard Studio dashboard that renders fine but slowly is no longer wrongly reported as blank — the assistant confirms the panels actually returned data before deciding, so it stops wasting a retry on a dashboard that was already correct. A genuinely blank dashboard is still caught. - **TrackMe panels only when they belong.** Fixed a rule that pushed a TrackMe feed-health panel onto every generated dashboard (and used a lookup that fails outside the TrackMe app). The assistant now adds a feed-health panel only when it's actually relevant, using a method that works in your app. --- ## 1.7.0 "ServiceNow integration" (included in the 1.8.0 release) > **Renamed to Adjutant AI.** The app is now **Adjutant AI** (formerly "AI Workbench"). > This is a **display-name change only** — the in-app title (the easter egg now lives on > the dot of the "i" in **Adjutant Ai**), the app label, the documentation, and the > assistant's own self-description all say **Adjutant AI**. Nothing functional changed: > the Splunk app id, your saved searches/dashboards/models, KVStore data, and generated > artifact names are unchanged, so the upgrade is seamless. **New — run playbooks automatically, and from other Splunk apps.** - **On a schedule or on an event.** A playbook can run **unattended** on a schedule (a "morning health check") or in response to a Splunk event — an alert, an ES correlation search, or an ITSI episode. When an event triggers it, the affected thing (the host, user, or entity in the alert) is handed to the playbook automatically, so it investigates exactly what fired. Two ready-made (disabled) examples are included to copy. - **Adjutant AI as a building block for other apps.** Other Splunk AI agents can now ask Adjutant AI to **list** and **run** your playbooks through a small, safe interface (an MCP server). Only playbooks you mark **MCPready** are exposed, every call must name the Org/BU it is for (which must be a business unit you have set up) as a safeguard, and runs go through the same governed, bounded service — never an open door. This interface is **off by default** — turn it on with one setting. When on, the tools can also appear inside **Splunk's own MCP Server**, reachable on the normal Splunk web address (no special port needed); you authenticate with a standard Splunk token. A ready-made, read-only **example playbook** ships enabled so there is always something to see the moment you switch the interface on. **New — "Report an issue" support packaging (all editions).** - One click on any conversation (per-turn 🐞, the Ask panel, or the new **Help tab**) packages exactly what happened — versions, the resolved prompt, the tools and model used, the generated dashboards/searches, and every error and warning — into a single file. - **Safe by construction:** secrets are stripped before anything leaves the browser, and the file is **encrypted** to the support key, so it's safe to send over any channel. - It even **tells you what kind of problem it looks like** and matches known issues, so simple cases are solved without a back-and-forth. - **Send it your way:** download it and attach it to your own ticket, use the built-in support form, or email it. The **Help tab** (Report + Documentation + About) is always reachable — even if the app is locked by licensing. **New — ServiceNow, done properly** (Professional + the `servicenow` feature). Read incidents, changes, problems and the **CMDB/CSDM** in plain English — with bounded blast-radius / dependency traversals ("what's the blast radius if this CI fails?"). Turn a Splunk alert, ITSI episode or ES notable into a rich, deterministically rendered ServiceNow incident and **write the number back** to the originating object (a re-fire updates, never duplicates; the closed-incident policy is configurable). **Security incidents (SIR)** with MITRE ATT&CK, off until an admin enables them. Two transports (REST **or** a ServiceNow MCP server), plus TISC threat-intel enrichment — all server-side and allowlisted, so ServiceNow can never block the assistant. *(Verified against the documented APIs and unit-tested; final certification is on a live ServiceNow.)* **New — run playbooks automatically, and from other apps.** Playbooks can run **unattended** on a schedule, or from a Splunk alert / ES correlation search / ITSI episode (the triggering entity is handed to the run). Adjutant AI can also expose **list / run** over an inbound **MCP server** (off by default, MCPready-only, Org/BU-scoped) — reachable inside Splunk's own MCP Server on the normal web address, with a standard Splunk token. **New — "Report an issue" support packaging (all editions).** One click packages a failing conversation — secret-stripped and **encrypted client-side** — with an automatic problem classification, plus an always-reachable **Help tab** even when the app is licence-locked. **New — Cribl Stream data-quality awareness** (Professional+). Reads Cribl's own forwarded logs and metrics to surface the timestamp / parse / dropped-event problems that happen *inside Cribl, before Splunk can see them* — the "green in Splunk but timestamped wrong" blind spot — folded into one readiness verdict. No Cribl Lake or Search required. **New — LLM reliability: retry, fallback & circuit breaker** (Enterprise). A brief provider hiccup (503 / 529 / rate-limit) auto-retries within a time budget; a per-config **circuit breaker** stops hammering a provider that's down, then probes for recovery; and an ordered **fallback** transparently switches to your next provider (and tells you which it used). Two new admin dashboards — **LLM Health** and **AI Activity** — plus per-user / BU / org concurrency caps, all conservative and off the critical path. **New — live model & cost catalogue (all editions).** Models and prices come from a runtime catalogue that updates without an app rebuild; **automatic model discovery** (Professional+) keeps it current without ever logging your keys; an Enterprise admin screen adds price overrides and manual model registration for private gateways. **Fixed.** Generated Simple XML dashboards now share a single base search across panels (faster) and get a top data-ingestion health panel; corrected a 3× Opus price over-charge (now server-side authoritative, with Opus 4.8 and Fable 5 included). --- ## 1.5.0 "Data Foundation & MCP OAuth" **New:** connect to **OAuth 2.1‑protected MCP servers** (authorization‑code + PKCE for interactive, client‑credentials for unattended; tokens held server‑side, never in the browser — see [MCP_OAUTH.md](MCP_OAUTH.md)); **onboard new data sources** — describe a source or attach a sample file and get a deployment‑ready add‑on package; a **"is my data parsed correctly?"** ingestion/timestamp check that reads Splunk's own internal logs; generated config **validated against your instance** and given a **0–100 Data Quality Score** (A–F); and attach a local sample file in Ask (only the file name is audited, never contents). **Improved:** works with the newest OpenAI "reasoning" models incl. Azure GPT‑5.4 / GPT‑5.4‑mini (auto‑detects the request format); more reliable generated dashboards; generated objects use the **`aiworkbench`** name tag; and Audit‑tab improvements (Business Unit column/filter, local‑timezone timestamps, reliable token/outcome capture). --- ## Earlier releases (1.0.0 – 1.4.3) - **1.4.3** — Clearer guidance and plain-language fixes when a free-tier LLM key hits its provider limits (e.g. Groq token-per-minute caps, Gemini zero-quota keys); the LLM config screen flags these up front. - **1.4.1** — Per-feature capability licensing with edition badges (Professional / Enterprise / MSP); gated features show a padlock, and nothing you created is ever deleted when a tier changes. Turn-level audit logging made reliable; more robust dashboard generation. - **1.4.0** — The assistant reads your own Splunk **live** (real search commands + installed visualizations) instead of guessing; Splunk Security Essentials detection content integrated. - **1.3.3** — TrackMe integration end-to-end (feed-health awareness + actions) with richer built-in platform knowledge. - **1.3.2** — First Splunkbase 1.x release: packaging and permissions hardening. - **1.3.1** — Fixed Org/BU edits dropping fields; safeguard to keep bundled playbooks correct after upgrades. - **1.3.0** — Real, per-Organisation audit logging of every AI interaction (Professional+). - **1.2.0** — Splunk Security Essentials content tools for playbooks. - **1.1.1** — Cisco Deep Time Series Model (CDTSM) playbooks: pre-trained anomaly detection and forecasting via the AI Toolkit, each with a proof dashboard. - **1.1.0** — Multi-tenancy and the Organisation / Business-Unit editor overhauled for clearer, safer tenant scoping. - **1.0.0** — The knowledge layer: ground answers in your organisation's own conventions. *(Releases before 1.0 are early pre-release history and are omitted here.)* --- ## Known issues - **Open the assistant from inside another app.** Adjutant AI is a "host shell": reach it from a navigation-menu entry inside Search, Enterprise Security, ITSI, or your own apps — not by clicking the app tile directly. Everything it creates lands in the namespace of the app you opened it from. - **Some Data Foundation features need self-hosted Splunk.** The configuration-reference grounding and config-package generation (1.5.0) read files on the Splunk server, so they are unavailable on Splunk Cloud; the assistant says so and continues with what it can. --- *When a published fix resolves a tracked GitHub issue, it is summarised here with its issue number — for example: "Fixed: a dashboard panel could display raw HTML markup as text instead of formatting it (#123)."*


Short Description:
AI agents that run inside your own Splunk, on the model you choose, including a local model with Ollama, so nothing has to leave your network. Ask in plain words and get a search, dashboard or alert that is run before it is saved. Once you switch it on, an agent investigates the moment an alert, ES notable or ITSI episode fires. Free for one user, no licence key.


Description:
Your Splunk team can do far more than it has time for. Adjutant AI gives them that time. Adjutant AI puts governed AI agents on the Splunk you already run. It ships with 67 ready-made agent templates, so you install it and start the same day: no prompts to write, no project to run. What changes for your team - Security analysts get back to the hard cases. Agents triage Enterprise Security notables and alerts with asset, identity and risk context, so your people start where the agent stopped. - Everyone else stops waiting for the SPL expert. Describe what you need in plain words and get a working search, dashboard or alert, checked on your own Splunk and owned by you. - The Splunk admin team finds problems sooner, and at lower cost. Agents check feed health, data quality and CIM coverage, explain any search with real row counts, and trace an ITSI service problem to its root cause from the data itself. - Managers can see what happened. Every step is shown live and can be stopped, every action is gated, and on Enterprise every run is audited. Your first week 1. Install the app and connect the AI model you choose: a cloud provider, or a local model on your own network for air-gapped sites. 2. Open the Console and run a ready-made agent on your own data: build a dashboard, explain a slow search, check a feed. 3. Switch on the agents that should work by themselves. When an alert, a notable or an ITSI episode fires, the investigation is already waiting when someone opens it. Be the team that got there first Splunk is one of the most valuable platforms in your organisation. Adjutant AI lets you show it: requests handled on the spot instead of in a ticket queue, investigations that start by themselves, and a Splunk team known for what it delivers. While others are still deciding whether AI belongs in their Splunk, you are already using it, under control. Built to be trusted Each agent works with the asking person's own Splunk permissions. Your keys stay on your side, and your data goes to no model but the one you choose. Runs on Splunk Enterprise and Splunk Cloud, alongside Enterprise Security, ITSI, the AI Toolkit, TrackMe and ServiceNow. Some agents need the Professional or Enterprise edition. Free for one user to build searches, dashboards and alerts, with no licence key needed. Your model, your network: Ollama or another local model, Azure OpenAI, Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, Bedrock and more. Keys stay in Splunk's secret store, and nothing is sent to us. Get started in three steps: install, connect your model with the setup wizard, ask your first question. Free for one user. For your team, request a 30-day Professional key: https://www.thedutchdatadifference.nl/contact/. Documentation: https://docs.thedutchdatadifference.nl/adjutant-ai/

### Highlights * **New configuration pages:** Accounts, DRP API, Proxy, Logging and Data Inputs. Accounts are checked against Group-IB when saved. * **Two data inputs:** *Violations* (confirmed violations by default) and *Typosquatting* (look-alike domain candidates), each with its own position and a Start From choice (last N days or a date). * **One event per revision** with the record's own timestamp; unchanged re-deliveries are not indexed again. Delete the old `[drp://]` stanza from `local/inputs.conf`.


Short Description:
Splunk application that collects your Group-IB Digital Risk Protection portfolio as structured events, with dashboards that show what is true now and what changed, and commands that act on it at Group-IB


Description:
Group-IB Digital Risk Protection watches the internet for abuse of your brands — phishing pages, fake shops, counterfeit listings, impersonating social accounts, rogue mobile apps — and runs the takedowns. This application brings that portfolio into Splunk beside the rest of your security data. This Splunk integration allows you to: - Collect two feeds, each with its own data input and sourcetype: Violations (confirmed violations) and Typosquatting (look-alike domain candidates). - Keep a change history, not duplicates: one event per revision, and a current-state store that answers "what is true now" in one lookup. - Watch the portfolio on seven dashboards, and be told by six alerts — among them Group-IB DRP - Act from the search bar: approve, reject or declare a violation with `| gibdrpapprove`, submit new ones with `| gibdrpupload`, read your brands and entitlements with `| gibdrpbrands` and `| gibdrpsubscription`, and maintain the app with `| gibdrpresync`, `| gibdrpcleanup` and `| gibdrploaddemo`. Every change sent to Group-IB is audited locally. To use this application you need an active Group-IB Digital Risk Protection subscription, a portal account with an API key, and Splunk Enterprise 9.2+ or Splunk Cloud.

No input needs a change when you upgrade. ## Compatibility | | Minimum | Tested with | | :------ | :----------------------- | :---------------- | | TheHive | 5.2.0 | 5.8.1 | | Cortex | 3.0.0 | 4.2.0 | | Splunk | 9.3 (Python 3.9 or 3.13) | Enterprise 10.2.1 | ## New * **Inputs continue where they stopped.** Until now each run asked TheHive for exactly the last interval and kept no state: a run that failed, hung or was skipped lost its window for good. Each pull now remembers the end of the last window it collected completely, in the KV store, and the next run continues from there. A TheHive outage of a few minutes is caught up by the next run, with no gap. * **Search head cluster:** only the captain collects; the others log `SKIP`. * **KV store disabled** (some heavy forwarders): the watermark is kept in the input's checkpoint directory on that instance, with a `KV` warning. * Two optional settings on the alerts & cases, audit, observables, tasks and timeline inputs: **lag_seconds** (default 60) and **max_catchup_seconds** (default 21600). ## Fixed * A collected object without `_createdAt` or `_updatedAt` no longer drops the whole run: it is indexed with the best date available, and `TH127` names the missing field. * A Splunk ES finding that annotates several techniques now gives one TTP per technique, instead of one procedure TheHive rejected. * A multivalue `ttp` field gives one TTP per value. * TheHive unreachable fails fast: connecting has its own 10 s timeout, and a request that timed out while reading is no longer sent again, so an alert can no longer be created twice. ## Upgrading * The first run after the upgrade creates the KV collection `thehive_cortex_checkpoints`; the add-on's role needs write access to it (`admin` and `sc_admin`, as in `default.meta`). * Events collected up to the upgrade are not collected again. * AppInspect: no failure and no error. One `check_for_custom_mako_templates` notice remains on `appserver/templates/base.html`, a file generated by the UCC framework. ## Thanks A big thank you to **Matt C** ([@mjc420](https://github.com/mjc420)), who found these problems running the add-on against TheHive 5.6.7 behind a proxy, and contributed the fixes and the watermark (pull requests #138 and #139). All of this release's fixes and the watermark are his work, and the commits keep his name. Full release notes: see `release_notes/v5.1.0.md` in the repos

item.title: CIM Assessment Toolkit (CAT) - v2.13.0 [Version Update]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
**v2.13.0 (October 26, 2026)** **Data Model Test columns** - The Results panel now shows the same columns as the Generated SPL, in the same order: \`Time\`, \`sourcetype\`, the common fields the dataset inherits from its base search (\`host\`, \`source\`, \`cim_entity_zone\`), then \`REQ\`, \`REC\`, and \`OPT\` markers in front of each tier's fields. Optional fields with no data appear as empty columns, so a missing field is visible instead of silently dropped. The Generated SPL no longer repeats \`sourcetype\` and lists the common fields ahead of the tier groups instead of inside the Optional group (CIM 8.7.0 declares \`\_time\`, \`host\`, \`source\`, \`sourcetype\`, and \`cim_entity_zone\` on about 30 datasets; the Splunk docs pages omit them). The Field Fill Rate and CIM Field Reference panels label those fields Tier \`Common\` and sort Common, Required, Recommended, Optional; both previously sorted the tier alphabetically, which put Optional first. **Send the report on demand** - New \`cim_validator_send_report_now\` report (\`| makeresults | sendalert email_report\`). Open it in Search and run it to email the CIM Assessment Report immediately. Any error appears in that job's search.log (Job -> Inspect Job), not in \`index\=\_internal\`. **Email failure is now a failure** \`email_report.py\` exits nonzero when the SMTP send fails, so \`sendmodalert\` logs the scheduled run as failed instead of success. **Troubleshooting** - Email Delivery Issues gains two rows: sign in to the sender mailbox first (an expired password returns the same \`535 5.7.3 Authentication unsuccessful\` as an SMTP AUTH block), and where ad hoc \`sendalert\` output goes. The \`cim_validator_coverage_collection\` description named the retired \`cim_validator_collection\` search; it now names \`cim_validator_collect\`. **v2.12.1 (October 26, 2026)** **Data Model Health app column** - The \`app\` column showed \`Splunk\` instead of \`Splunk_SA_CIM\` because the summary name \`tstats:DM_Splunk_SA_CIM\_\\` was split at the first underscore. The Data Model Health tab and \`cim_validator_acceleration_health\` now take the owning app and model name from \`/services/data/models\`, so any app name works, including custom add-ons that ship their own accelerated models. The Avg Run and P90 Run columns key on the full acceleration search name for the same reason. \- **\*\*Earliest and Latest columns\*\*** -- Both showed N/A for every model on search heads where the summarization endpoint reports times as ISO 8601 strings rather than epoch seconds. The dashboard, the saved search, and the report's acceleration section now accept either form. \- **\*\*Run times without \`\_internal\`\*\*** -- Avg Run and P90 Run on the Data Model Health tab and in \`cim_validator_acceleration_health\` came from a 7-day search of \`index\=\_internal\` scheduler logs, which is empty for users without access to that index (common on managed ES search heads). They now read \`summary.average_time\` and \`summary.p90\` from the summarization endpoint, which Splunk maintains for every accelerated model, so the columns fill for anyone who can open the tab. N/A appears only when Splunk has not recorded a run yet. \- **\*\*TA Inventory view\*\*** -- New view (menu bar: TA Inventory) with four exportable tables. Observed CIM Coverage lists every sourcetype with events in a CIM data model, with its models, indexes, and tags, read from the summary index so it is instant. Configured CIM Coverage walks eventtypes, tags, props, and CIM data model constraints through REST to show which add-ons are configured to normalize which sourcetypes into which models, with events seen in range (0 means configured but no data). Sourcetypes Missing from Inventory lists mapped sourcetypes absent from \`cim_sourcetype_inventory\`. Installed Splunk Apps mirrors Manage Apps (name, folder, version, update checking, visibility, sharing, status, derived app origin, update available) for sharing with a CIM reviewer. \- **\*\*Collection writes observed tags\*\*** -- Each dataset job now also records the CIM tags carried by every index/sourcetype as one \`ReportType\=cim_observed_tags\` row per model/dataset/index/sourcetype. No new search jobs; the tags ride along in the existing \`tstats\`. The dashboard base search filters on \`cim_validator_v2\`, so existing panels and the report are unaffected. The Observed table fills after the first collection run on 2.12.1. \- **\*\*Data model retention reads the effective value\*\*** -- Retention (days) on the Data Model Health tab and in \`cim_validator_acceleration_health\` came from \`/services/data/models\`, which returns one row per \`datamodels.conf\` layer; with two apps setting \`acceleration.earliest_time\` the panel showed whichever row came first. It now uses the summarization endpoint's effective range, falling back to the merged \`conf-datamodels\` value, and a new Retention Conflict column lists every app and value when layers disagree. \- **\*\*Tier markers in Data Model Test SPL\*\*** -- The Generated SPL places \`REQ\`, \`REC\`, and \`OPT\` marker columns in front of the Required, Recommended, and Optional field groups so a reviewer can see where each tier begins. Only tiers with fields get a marker. Suggested by NS2 Security Ops during a CAT walkthrough. **v2.11.1 (October 20, 2026)** \- **\*\*Scope filter honors sourcetype inventory\*\*** -- The quality KPIs, the CIM Compliance tab, the Remediation Priorities tab, and the automated report filtered by data model category only, so a sourcetype the inventory marks operational (for example \`snow:sysevents\`, mapped to Change, whose category is security and operational) counted under the Security scope. All of them now also check the sourcetype's inventory scope; only sourcetypes missing from the inventory fall back to the model category. \- **\*\*Exclusions report enriched\*\*** -- \`cim_sourcetype_exclusions_search\` now joins each excluded sourcetype to \`cim_sourcetype_inventory\` (tech category, scope, security relevance, data models, vendor, description, expanded description, provenance) so exclusions can be reviewed in context. Sourcetypes missing from the inventory still appear with blank enrichment columns. \- **\*\*CIM Coverage honors sourcetype inventory\*\*** -- The CIM Coverage KPI, its daily trend collection, and the report counted a sourcetype as mapped only when it mapped to a model in the selected scope's category, so a security sourcetype mapped only to an operational model counted as unmapped and the KPI disagreed with the Unmapped Data tab. All three now count by the sourcetype's inventory scope, and mapped means mapped to any CIM model. Sourcetypes missing from the inventory fall back to the categories of the models they map to; the Unmapped Data tab applies the same fallback.


Short Description:
Measure and validate Splunk CIM compliance at the data model and dataset level — with field-mapping quality scoring, unmapped data discovery, prescribed-value validation, remediation priorities, data model testing, TA sourcetype coverage and inventory, and automated reporting.


Description:
The CIM Assessment Toolkit (CAT) measures and validates Common Information Model (CIM) compliance across your Splunk data models at the data model + dataset level. CAT scores field-mapping quality, data quality, and prescribed-value compliance; surfaces unmapped sourcetypes and impact-ranked remediation priorities; monitors data model acceleration health; and generates professional Word-document reports with optional scheduled email delivery. A new feature is four TA Inventory tables which reveal what TAs cover which sourcetypes for CIM normalization and their versions - essential information for maintaining CIM normalization coverage.

Version 1.0.3 - reliability and bug-fix release Fixes \- Cursor pagination no longer stops early when the API returns a cursor value of 0. \- Malformed Retry-After headers no longer stop collection. \- {{checkpoint}} and other placeholders are now URL-encoded in the URL and form-encoded in form bodies (fixes timestamps with "+" offsets). \- JSON bodies with unquoted placeholders, e.g. {"min_id": {{checkpoint}}}, are now accepted; an empty value is sent as null. \- Short-lived OAuth tokens (under 60 seconds) are reused instead of being requested before every call. \- Temporary token-endpoint errors (429, 5xx, network) are retried automatically. \- Very large numeric IDs are stored exactly (no rounding). \- If a page fails partway through a run, events already collected are not collected again (oldest-first APIs). \- Checkpoints keep working when KV Store is disabled or unavailable (local file fallback). \- Windows: token refresh no longer times out when two inputs share an account. \- License notices no longer reappear in Splunk Messages on every run. Improvements \- Warning in the logs when the Events path is not found, listing the fields the API returned. \- Fewer token-store lookups per run. \- Python settings updated for Splunk 10.2 and later; earlier versions remain supported. Upgrade: install over the previous version. Accounts, inputs, checkpoints and license keys are kept.


Short Description:
Collects data from any REST or JSON API through a modular input with comprehensive authentication support, configurable pagination, and KV Store checkpointing.


Description:
ROVIX Universal API Add-on for Splunk lets you bring data from any REST/JSON API into Splunk by filling in forms. No code or custom scripts are needed. The problem it solves Security and IT teams need data from dozens of cloud services: identity providers, EDR tools, SaaS platforms, threat-intelligence feeds and internal APIs. Many of these have no Splunk add-on, or the add-on is outdated or limited. The usual workarounds are custom Python scripts or one-off modular inputs. Each one handles OAuth tokens, pagination and “what did I already collect?” differently, breaks when a token expires, and is hard to maintain or hand over. What the add-on does One place for every API. Define an account (credentials and authentication) once, then create as many inputs as you need. Each input has its own endpoint, interval, index and sourcetype. Handles authentication for you. Supports OAuth 2.0 (client credentials, authorization code with automatic refresh-token rotation, password grant), JWT bearer and private_key_jwt (including Google service accounts), session login, HMAC request signing, API key, bearer token, Basic and Digest, plus mTLS. Tokens are stored encrypted in Splunk, refreshed before they expire, and renewed automatically if the API rejects them. Collects everything, exactly once. Built-in pagination (offset, page, cursor, Link header, next URL) fetches every page. Checkpoints in the KV Store pick up where the last run stopped, and only move forward after a run completes successfully, so data isn’t skipped. Built to keep running. Retries with back-off on rate limits (HTTP 429) and server errors, honouring Retry-After. A monitoring dashboard and per-input logs make problems easy to see. Who it’s for: Splunk admins and SOC teams who need to onboard API-based data sources quickly and reliably on Splunk Enterprise or Splunk Cloud Platform, without writing and maintaining code. Licensing: a 30-day free evaluation with all features is included, then a per-server license key, verified offline. The add-on runs entirely inside your Splunk environment and sends no data to Rovix Technologies. Developed by Rovix Technologies Pvt. Ltd. Contact: info@RovixTechnologies.com

item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
**Splunk MCP Server 2.1.0** Splunk MCP Server 2.1.0 adds tools for retrieving fired alert results, checking alert action status, and finding silent alerts. It also introduces self-service encrypted token management, updated management pages, stronger authentication, and improved telemetry. **What's New** **Alert Investigation** Added three tools for investigating Splunk alerts: * splunk_get_fired_alert_results * splunk_get_alert_action_status * splunk_find_silent_alerts Use these tools to retrieve retained search results for a specific alert firing, check recorded alert action outcomes, and find enabled alerts with no recorded firings. Fired alert results and silent alert discovery support pagination. Silent alert discovery also supports app filtering and a lookback window of up to 90 days. **Encrypted Token Management** * Added self-service token management for non-admin users with the mcp_edit_tokens_own capability. Creating, activating, deactivating, and deleting tokens also requires Splunk’s edit_tokens_own capability. * Users can create, list, activate, deactivate, and delete tokens they create for themselves, and view token status, expiration, and recorded last-use information. * Administrators can manage tokens across users, subject to native Splunk token permissions, and generate or delete the shared encryption key pair. * All encrypted MCP tokens use the public key from this administrator-managed key pair. * Added configurable key expiration, with a default validity of 180 days and a maximum of 365 days. Newly created tokens cannot outlive the key. **Management Interface Improvements** * Updated the Tools page with search, sorting, filters, and bulk activation and deactivation. * Updated the Usage dashboard and changed its default time range to 7 days. * Moved allowed SPL commands and server settings into separate Commands and Server pages. * Added support for Splunk light and dark themes. **Security and Telemetry Improvements** * Strengthened authentication for tool-management operations. * Added token audit events and more context to administrative logs. * Improved logging for SPL errors and failed tool calls. **Issues Fixed** * Fixed splunk_get_indexes to include search-peer indexes while preserving pagination. * Fixed Gemini compatibility with alert severity schemas. * Fixed request recovery after increasing the MCP request timeout. * Fixed an endpoint URL locale mismatch that affected OAuth connections. * Fixed cleanup after failed encrypted-token registration. **Upgrade Considerations** * Direct MCP bearer-token connections now require credentials encrypted with the current server key. Plaintext and previous-key support are removed, along with the require_encrypted_token and legacy_token_grace_days settings. * Existing keys without expiration receive 180-day validity when initialized after upgrade. Existing expiration dates are preserved. * Deactivate all non-expired registered tokens before deleting the shared encryption key pair. After generating a replacement pair, issue new tokens and update clients. * Non-admin users need mcp_edit_tokens_own to access self-service token management and edit_tokens_own to create, activate, deactivate, or delete their own tokens. * Existing tokens are not automatically added to the new registry. The self-service token list shows tokens created by the current user. * Token API integrations must use /services/mcp_token/tokens and /services/mcp_token/key-pair instead of the previous creation and rotation operations at /services/mcp_token. * splunk_find_silent_alerts requires access to \_audit. splunk_get_alert_action_status requires access to the relevant \_internal action logs. * splunk_get_fired_alert_results requires retained search-job results. Expired results are reported as unavailable.


Description:

It acts as a universal adapter allowing AI systems to access, execute, and integrate functionalities from diverse systems through a common protocol, simplifying data sharing and tool interoperability without custom coding for each integration. Splunk's Model Context Protocol (MCP) server leverages this to provide a standardized, secure, and scalable interface to connect AI assistants, agents, and other intelligent systems with data in the Splunk platform for both Enterprise & Cloud customers in beta. 🔑 Key Features - Universal Connectivity Seamlessly connects AI agents and tools to Splunk data resources in a secure and efficient manner. - Enterprise-Grade Security Includes built-in authentication, authorization, and Role-Based Access Control (RBAC). - Rapid Deployment Offers a plug-and-play solution, eliminating the need for custom integrations. ⚙️ Core Capabilities - Explore the Data Navigate and interact with Splunk data effortlessly. - Discover Knowledge Objects Identify and access relevant saved searches, lookups, and other knowledge assets. - Execute Searches Run powerful Splunk queries to extract insights and drive intelligent workflows. - Leverage AI capabilities from Splunk’s AI Assistant for SPL & MLTK SPL search generation from natural language, search optimization, search explanation, retrieve MLTK models and algorithms.
